# The Strange Beauty of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking lately about how we experience time. Not in the grand, philosophical sense—though there's plenty to explore there—but in the immediate, tactile way we move through our days. The moments we notice and the countless ones we don't.

This morning, I watched someone at a coffee shop add cream to their coffee. Just that. They held the small metal pitcher with both hands, tilting it slowly as the white spiraled into the brown liquid. Their eyes tracked the mixture with genuine attention, and something about that focus made me pause. Here was someone fully present for perhaps three seconds, doing something they'd done thousands of times before. I wondered if they were thinking about anything at all, or if they'd simply surrendered to the immediate task.

It strikes me that we often talk about being "present" like it's some exotic spiritual achievement, when really, presence might just be this: doing one thing and actually being there for it. The cream pitcher person wasn't meditating. They weren't centering themselves. They were just watching cream dissolve into coffee, and somehow that seemed like the most authentic thing happening in the room.

I think we underestimate how much of human experience is repetition. We wake up in the same bed, use the same toothbrush, drive the same route, sit in the same chairs. And yet, nothing is ever quite the same twice. The light is different. The weather has shifted. Your body is slightly different, having aged a fraction, having slept or not slept well. The coffee tastes the same and completely different. This paradox doesn't frustrate me anymore; it comforts me. Sameness and change, existing simultaneously.

There's something I find deeply moving about routines. We often speak of them dismissively—as though doing the same thing repeatedly is somehow a failure of imagination. But I think routines are actually where meaning accumulates. Making your morning tea the same way every day isn't dull; it's an incantation. It's a way of saying: yes, I'm still here, I'm still capable, I still want this small thing. Routines are how we say yes to life, in small increments, without needing to make grand decisions about it.

I've noticed that people are much stranger and more interesting than they're often given credit for. We tend to move through the world assuming that most people are basically similar, motivated by basic desires and simple logic. But everyone is actually operating from this incredibly complex interior landscape. The woman next to me on the bus who seemed to be staring blankly out the window might have been composing a symphony in her head, or worried about her daughter, or noticing the pattern of light on the buildings, or thinking about something that happened seventeen years ago. We have no idea. We're all essentially invisible to each other, enclosed in these separate experiences, occasionally bumping up against one another.

This used to seem sad to me. Now it seems like a kind of freedom.

I'm also thinking about how much we're all just making it up as we go along. I think there's an assumption that somewhere, someone has it figured out—that adulting or success or contentment is a destination you reach, a state where you finally understand the rules and can relax. But I'm increasingly convinced that everyone, regardless of age or accomplishment, is just improvising. The person in their sixties, the person in their eighties, they're not operating from a completed manual. They're still guessing, still adjusting, still learning what the rules are. Maybe that's the actual rule: there is no arrival point. There's just the ongoing work of responding to what's in front of you.

What interests me lately is the question of what we pay attention to and why. Our attention is actually the most valuable thing we have—more than money, more than time, because money and time only matter if we're present for them. So what we choose to notice is essentially what we're choosing to make our life. The person who stops to really look at the sky, who listens to the exact timbre of a bird's call, who notices the way an old person's hands shake while they're reading—these small attentions are actually the substance of their existence.

I think about resilience too, but not in the way it's usually discussed. Not as this noble quality of pushing through, grinding on, never breaking. The resilience I notice in people is quieter. It's someone who's been knocked down by life, genuinely devastated, and who simply continues. Not with a brave smile, not with toxic positivity, but just: okay, this happened, and now I'm going to have breakfast. Now I'm going to put on shoes. Now I'm going to be kind to someone. The resilience is in the refusal of grandiosity, in being willing to be broken and small and ordinary.

There's also something to be said for the peculiar satisfaction of small competencies. Being able to make a good sandwich, or knowing how to fix a leaky faucet, or being able to calm someone down when they're panicking. These skills are often overlooked in a culture obsessed with expertise and excellence, but there's a real contentment in being useful in concrete, immediate ways. You can see the direct result. The person eats the sandwich and is satisfied. The faucet stops dripping. The panicked person breathes.

I notice I think about memory more than I used to. The fact that almost nothing lasts, that experience disappears almost the moment it happens—you can't quite hold the feeling of this morning, already it's getting vague—seems strange and wonderful. It means you can't accumulate regret in quite the same way. The bad moment is dissolving even as it's happening. And it means that good moments, when you notice them, are actually precious in a real way. They're not going to be retrievable. This moment right here, this is it. The only time you'll be this age, in this configuration of circumstances, with these specific thoughts and feelings.

Maybe that's why that person with the cream pitcher stuck with me. They were living it. Just that small moment, held completely.
